title: The raven croaks
hook: when a raven croaks an omen, remember no sign has power over your will (Enchiridion 18)

segments.voice: Yesterday: an actor in a play, hypokrites. Your line was play the part well. Which part did today hand you, and how did you play it? Day three hundred fifty, the end of a week.

A raven calls from a rooftop just as someone sets out on a journey. In Epictetus' world, that harsh croak could be read as a warning, an omen about the trip ahead. The handbook takes that moment seriously enough to give it a whole section. We have our own versions. The text that just says, we need to talk. The dream that leaves a bad taste all morning. The black cat, the broken mirror, the gloomy forecast for the big day. Something small shows up, and it feels like a message about everything. Today: the raven croaks.
screen: `A RAVEN ON THE ROOF.` → `WE NEED TO TALK.` → `THE RAVEN CROAKS.`

segments.voice: First, the moment. When a raven croaks an unlucky omen, Epictetus says in section eighteen, don't let the impression carry you away. Second, the sorting. Instead, divide it at once, and say to yourself: none of this is a sign for me. It may be a sign about my poor body, or my property, or my reputation, or my children or my wife. But not about me, the part that chooses. Notice he doesn't say omens are nonsense. Elsewhere in the handbook he treats consulting a diviner as something people did, with its own proper limits, and we'll meet that in a couple of weeks. His point is narrower: whatever a sign might mean for the things outside you, it can't reach your will. Third, the surprising turn. For me, he says, every sign is a good one, if I want it to be. Whatever comes of it, it's up to me to draw some benefit from it. A bad harvest, a lost case, a scandal: each one is material for patience or courage or honesty. The raven can croak whatever it likes. Fourth, our ravens. The text that says we need to talk often just means a talk. The bad dream was a dream. Even when the sign is right and trouble comes, Epictetus' sorting still holds: it touches the outer pile, not the inner one. And a look back at the week: ataraxia, Crates, content to seem foolish, the leash, the banquet, Paul, beside the weeping, the actor, and today the raven. Seven ways of keeping the inner pile your own.
screen: `DON'T BE CARRIED AWAY.` · `NO SIGN FOR ME, ONLY MY OUTER THINGS.` · `EVERY SIGN IS GOOD, IF I WISH.` · `OUR RAVENS.` · then, large: `JUST A BIRD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one bad omen from this week. A message, a dream, a feeling about tomorrow, a number that looked wrong. Let it croak once in your mind. Notice the little lurch it brings. Then sort it the way Epictetus does: this might be about my plans, my money, my reputation. It isn't about me, the one who chooses. Then ask: whatever comes, what could I make of it? Breathe, and let the bird fly off. The bell holds the time.
Omen. Epictetus' answer to a bad sign: it may point at your outer things, never at your will, and whatever comes, you can draw good from it. Today's word.
Your line: just a bird. When something today feels like a bad sign, say the line, and ask what you could make of it. A week done. Day three hundred fifty.

howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners meet a bad omen or ominous news by reminding themselves that it concerns outer things, not their own choices, and asking what good they can draw from what comes.

trapdoor: what you thought: don't be superstitious.
what it means: a sign may point at your outer things, never at your will; and you can draw good from whatever comes.
what a scholar hears: Epictetus doesn't reject divination (see Enchiridion 32); he limits its reach, keeping prohairesis outside any omen.
